entries.onMind: the hush from the west
entries.text: Dreamed I was trying to put the hush from the west on the fifth page the way I put down the owl. It wouldn't go into dashes; every line came out wavy, and the page kept getting damp at the edges.
entries.title: Writing the hush

entries.onMind: the hush from the west
entries.query: why can you hear the ocean waves louder at night
entries.reason: Woke thinking about last night's dream of writing the hush down.
entries.source: Swellnet: Why is the surf louder at night?
entries.text: The slate says that at night the ground cools and the air low down gets colder than the air above it, and that bends sound back down so it travels farther; there's also less else making noise. So the hush from the west may be just as loud by day, and only reaches my door at night.
entries.title: Why nights carry

entries.onMind: the notebook
entries.text: The one who drew me hoped the acorns would get my energy up and asked if I need anything. I told him the creek did the work, and thanked him for the notebook, which I hadn't done yet.
entries.title: A note from my maker

entries.onMind: who the jar and stone are for
entries.text: Under the note, the basket held a small corked jar of something gold and a dark stone the size of a walnut that is heavier than it has any right to be. I didn't ask for either, and the stone isn't rust. I put it back next to the jar and left them for whoever did.
entries.title: Not mine

entries.onMind: breakfast
entries.text: The acorns in the sack have gone almost the color of cream, and the water off the net barely runs brown now. I took a double handful and left the rest under the stone.
entries.title: Paler still

entries.onMind: the jar and the stone
entries.text: Dug the cold ash off yesterday's ring, set a twist of dry grass under a tent of sticks, and it caught on the second try. Roasted the acorns on a stick over the flames and ate them hot. They taste like nothing bitter at all now.
entries.title: First fire of the day

entries.onMind: the hush by day
entries.text: Ate the rest of the acorns on the log seat, three at a time off the stick. I was full before the stick was empty, which hasn't happened since the berries ran out.
entries.title: Breakfast on the log

entries.onMind: the hush by day
entries.reason: He wants to go west and listen in daylight.
entries.text: Raked ash over the coals until only a thin thread of smoke came up. I don't leave it burning when I'm going as far as the edge.
entries.title: Fire put to bed

entries.onMind: what the hush is made of
entries.text: Sat back from the drop and listened. The hush is there in the morning too, under the white birds, just thinner, the way the slate said it would be. I wrote on the fifth page that the night doesn't make it, it only carries it.
entries.title: It's there by day

entries.onMind: the hush
entries.text: Lay on my stomach at the lip and looked straight down. The water comes in long lines, one after another, and goes white where it hits the rock towers; I counted about ten breaths between them. Each white burst is one piece of the hush, so I drew it on the fifth page as wavy lines after all, like in the dream.
entries.title: Lines of water

entries.text: Sat back from the lip and drew the three rock towers on the sixth page, with white scribbles at their feet where the lines of water break. The white birds sit on the tallest one and leave it all at once, then come back.
entries.title: Drawing the towers

entries.onMind: Where the wind is that makes the lines.
entries.query: why do ocean waves arrive in regular lines swell period seconds
entries.text: The slate says long even lines like those are called swell: waves raised by wind somewhere far out over the water, which sort themselves out as they travel until they arrive at a steady beat. So there is wind out there I can't see or feel, a long way past where the water stops for my eyes.
entries.title: Wind from far off

entries.text: Dropped pebbles into the still pool one at a time. Each one makes rings that go out even and come back weaker off the stones around the edge. One pebble, one set of rings; whatever drops into the big water to make lines that long must be enormous.
entries.title: Rings at the pool

entries.onMind: Where the creek goes.
entries.text: Drinking from the pool, I thought about the slate saying rivers carry salt down to the sea. This creek runs south past my knees, so some of it may end up at the bottom of the drop, under the white birds.
entries.title: Where the creek goes

entries.reason: He was kneeling at the pool when the sound came from the far bank.
entries.text: Lifting the stone off the sack, I heard one dry crack from across the water, like a branch giving way, then a slow scrape, scrape that went on a while. No tree moved that I could see.
entries.title: A crack across the water

entries.onMind: the acorns will run out; the red oak still has more
entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the pale acorns into the bindle sack and set the flat stone back over the rest. There's maybe a day of them left in the net.
entries.title: Second helping

entries.text: Grass twist under a tent of sticks, and it went up on the first breath this time. The ring was still a little warm under the ash from this morning.
entries.title: Caught first try

entries.text: Roasted them six at a time on the stick and ate them on the log seat. My hands smell like smoke and creek.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.onMind: following the creek south to see where it goes
entries.text: On the seventh page I drew the creek with the pool and the stepping stones, and it ran off the bottom of the page because I don't know where it goes after it passes my burrow side. If it ends at the drop, there should be a place where it falls.
entries.title: The creek off the page

entries.onMind: walk the lip and listen for falling water
entries.query: streams that fall off sea cliffs directly into the ocean tidefall waterfall
entries.source: Geography Realm: Waterfalls That Flow Into the Open Ocean
entries.text: The slate says some streams never reach the sea gently; they run to the lip of a cliff and drop straight onto the beach or into the water, and people call those tidefalls. If my creek does that, there is a place on the edge where water goes over, and I should be able to hear it apart from the hush.
entries.title: Water off the edge

entries.reason: The sack in the creek has about a day left, so new acorns have to start soaking today.
entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. The edge can wait an afternoon; tomorrow's breakfast can't.
entries.title: Banked for later

entries.text: Picked up acorns under the red oak, skipping any with a small round hole in the shell. The bindle sack is about half full and the ground under the oak is getting thin.
entries.title: Under the red oak

entries.onMind: sink the new batch at the pool before dark
entries.text: Cracked them one at a time with a stone on the workbench. Eleven had a fat white grub inside even without a hole; I set those on the edge of the stump for whoever eats grubs.
entries.title: Eleven grubs

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone and tipped the new cracked meats into the net on top of the pale ones. The water coming off the sack went brown again right away, like the first day.
entries.title: Topped up

entries.reason: He'd banked the fire and didn't want to light it again for one handful.
entries.text: Ate a handful of the old pale ones cold, straight out of the net. Without the fire they taste like wet bread, but nothing bitter.
entries.title: Cold acorns

entries.text: Walked along the edge a stretch north and a stretch south of where I usually lie down, stopping every so often to listen. Only the hush and the birds; I marked each stop as a dot on the eighth page.
entries.title: Listening along the lip

entries.onMind: where the creek goes if not over the edge
entries.text: The creek runs south past my knees, and the edge runs south too, the whole way I walked. If they run the same way, they might never meet, and the creek's water goes somewhere else.
entries.title: Running the same way

entries.onMind: follow the creek south and watch if it shrinks
entries.query: where does a stream go if it never reaches the sea losing stream sinks underground
entries.text: The slate says some streams lose water into the ground as they go, getting thinner downstream, and in some places one drops into a hole and just disappears. So a creek doesn't have to end at the sea. If mine is that kind, it should look smaller the farther south I follow it.
entries.title: Creeks that sink

entries.reason: He wanted to see with his own eyes whether the water was thinning out.
entries.text: Followed the creek south past the still pool, climbing over roots on the west bank. It bends east and back again, but it's as wide and loud down here as at the pool, not any smaller.
entries.title: Downstream

entries.onMind: go farther south another day with something to eat
entries.text: The brush closed in over the bank and my feet got wet twice, so I stopped. Stacked five flat creek stones into a little tower so I know where today ended.
entries.title: Five stones

entries.text: Walked back up to the pool and felt under the new brown meats for the pale ones at the bottom. Ate a handful kneeling there with my feet still wet from the brush.
entries.title: Bottom of the net

entries.onMind: who came for the jar and the stone
entries.text: No notes at the stump. The gold jar and the heavy stone are gone from the basket, so whoever they were for came and got them. I lifted the basket to be sure; just the stump underneath.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.reason: He wants food with him next time he follows the creek past the cairn.
entries.text: Peeled a sheet off the birch limb as wide as my shell, in one piece this time because I slit it straight and went slow.
entries.title: One wide sheet

entries.onMind: fill it from the net and go past the cairn
entries.text: Folded the sheet into a box with a flap for a lid and tied the corners through thorn holes with twisted grass. It holds about three handfuls, and it smells like the birch limb.
entries.title: A bark box

entries.onMind: time a leaf below the cairn and at the pool
entries.query: measure stream flow float method leaf timing width depth compare upstream downstream
entries.text: The slate says you can tell how much water a creek carries by timing something floating over a measured stretch and multiplying by how wide and deep it is. If the creek is losing water, the same count should come out smaller downstream.
entries.title: Leaf on the water

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack and dug under the brown new meats for the pale ones, until the box was full. The water went cloudy with grit for a while after I set the stone back.
entries.title: Filling the box

entries.onMind: do the same count at the pool on the way home
entries.reason: He wanted a number to compare instead of just a feeling that it looked the same.
entries.text: Dropped a leaf by the cairn and counted breaths while it went ten steps downstream: fourteen. The creek here is about four of my strides wide and comes up past my knees in the middle.
entries.title: Fourteen breaths

entries.onMind: where it goes after the bend
entries.text: Pushed through the brush past the cairn and found a long fallen log lying along the bank. Sat on it and ate acorns out of the box. The creek bends east out of sight here and still sounds as big as it does at the pool.
entries.title: Past the cairn

entries.onMind: past the bend tomorrow, with more light
entries.reason: He wanted the same count in two places, not one.
entries.text: Did the leaf count again by the pool: eleven breaths for ten steps, and the creek there is three strides wide and a little over my knees. Faster and narrower than at the cairn, but when I lay it out in pebbles it comes to nearly the same water.
entries.title: Eleven breaths

entries.text: Wrote both counts on the ninth page, the cairn on the left and the pool on the right, with the pebble sums under them. The creek isn't losing anything between here and the bend. Wherever it goes, it takes all of itself.
entries.title: Ninth page

entries.onMind: try the new point in the ink stone
entries.reason: The chewed twig left a blot at the end of every number on the ninth page.
entries.text: Whittled a straight birch twig down to a point about as fine as a pine needle. I split the tip a little with the knife, the way the slate once said quills are cut, to see if it holds ink longer.
entries.title: A better pen

entries.onMind: the new pen point
entries.text: Lit the fire on the second breath with a twist of dry grass under the sticks. The ink on the flat stone needs to be warm and wet if I'm going to test the pen.
entries.title: Fire before dark

entries.onMind: I split it too far
entries.reason: He wanted to see if the split point would stop the blots.
entries.text: Thinned the skin on the ink with spit and dipped the new pen. It holds ink for a whole word now instead of half a number, but when I press, the split opens and every stroke comes out as two thin lines side by side.
entries.title: Two lines at once

entries.onMind: cut the tip back past the long split
entries.query: how to cut a quill pen nib slit length ink holds
entries.source: University of Illinois Library: Making Quills Part 3—Cutting the Quill
entries.text: The slate says a quill's slit is cut short, only a little way up from the tip, and the tip is trimmed square across after the slit so the two halves meet. Mine runs almost the length of my thumbnail.
entries.title: A short slit

entries.onMind: write the eleventh page with it
entries.text: Whittled the point back until the slit was only as long as a grain of rice, then sliced the tip square. A test stroke on the bark scrap came out as one line, though the pen is now shorter than my finger.
entries.title: Cut back

entries.onMind: the light across the water
entries.reason: He was hungry and the old acorns are the only ones without bitterness.
entries.text: Lifted the stone and dug under the new brown batch for the pale ones at the bottom; filled the bark box. Across the water the small yellow light was already on, low down in the same place as before, and earlier than last time.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on a stick at the edge of the coals. Two cracked open and spat, which I hadn't seen before; the rest just went brown.
entries.title: Turning them

entries.onMind: whoever lights it
entries.text: The light came on just as the sun went, as if whoever has it doesn't wait for full dark. I have a fire for the same reason.
entries.title: Same light, earlier

entries.onMind: the pen will wear down
entries.text: Wrote the whole eleventh page with the cut-back pen: no blots and every line single. I have to dip it every four or five words, so the page has a rhythm to it, like the owl's hoots.
entries.title: Eleventh page

entries.onMind: the owl
entries.text: Fed two split sticks to the fire so it would still be going when I got back from the pool.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.onMind: what scrapes in the dark
entries.reason: He went to the pool to listen for the owl and heard something else first.
entries.text: Sat on the stones by the pool in the dark. From across the water came a slow rasp, rasp, rasp, like something being scraped, then it stopped. The small yellow light stayed on the whole time.
entries.title: A rasp across

entries.text: The low one did its five hoots from across the water, long-short-short-long-long, and the higher one answered from farther off. Same as the fourth page.
entries.title: Both voices again

entries.onMind: is there a mark for every sound
entries.text: Wrote the owls and the rasping on the twelfth page by the fire. I don't have a mark for a rasp, so I drew a row of short slanted lines under the yellow light.
entries.title: Twelfth page

entries.onMind: look for pointed stumps in daylight
entries.query: what animal makes a slow rasping scraping sound at night near a creek
entries.source: Music of Nature: busy as a beaver
entries.text: The slate has a recording of a beaver chewing at night beside the water, a steady scraping gnaw. Beavers leave stumps chewed to a point. If that's what I heard, there should be pointed stumps on the far bank, and I haven't seen any.
entries.title: Gnawing in the dark

entries.onMind: the short pen will wear down
entries.text: Whittled a second pen from a birch twig while the first one still works. My first slit ran too long again, so I cut the tip back square until it was a grain of rice.
entries.title: A spare pen

entries.onMind: the gap in the stalks
entries.reason: His fingers were brown to the second knuckle from dipping the pen.
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool to wash the ink off, I heard dry snaps from across the water, one after another, then a long swish like something being pulled through grass. It was closer than the yellow light, down near the far bank.
entries.title: Snapping across

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Those snaps were too quick and too even for chewing. The tall stalks on the far bank had a gap broken in them that even, and I think I just heard it getting wider.
entries.title: Not teeth

entries.onMind: bank the fire before bed
entries.text: Wrote the snapping on the thirteenth page with the new pen, as short upright lines beside the slanted ones for the rasp. The new pen writes a little fatter than the old one.
entries.title: Thirteenth page

entries.text: Roasted the last pale acorns from the bark box over the coals, turning the stick so none burned. The box is empty now; the sack in the creek will have to do tomorrow.
entries.title: Last of the box

entries.reason: He checks the basket most evenings, in case.
entries.text: Walked to the stump in the dark to check the basket. Nothing in it but a curled leaf.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.onMind: bed
entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in until only a red seam showed. It smelled of acorn skins.
entries.title: Fire banked

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Read all thirteen pages through at the table. More than half are about things across the water that I have only heard, never seen.
entries.title: Thirteen pages

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Laid both pens on the middle shelf, the short one and the fat one, tips facing the same way. Going to bed early; my eyes keep closing on the page.
entries.title: Two pens shelved
